claims.claim: Rivera argues Martin's archaic diction works because each old term sits in a context that lets the reader decipher its older meaning without disruption.
claims.source: A. R. Rivera, 'A Brief Linguistic Exam of A Song Of Ice And Fire', 10 September 2023
claims.quote: archaic diction, but synonymy and antonymy, semantic shifts
claims.page: opening paragraph and the paragraph on 'elsewise' and 'without'

claims.claim: Peterson states that as of 21 September 2011 the Dothraki he built had reached 3,163 words.
claims.source: David J. Peterson, 'The Header Script', Dothraki.com, 21 September 2011
claims.quote: Dothraki is now up to 3,163 words

claims.claim: Peterson treats the spellings of the Dothraki words printed in Martin's books as canon that his own language had to accommodate.
claims.source: David J. Peterson, 'Developing Canon', Dothraki.com, 18 March 2012
claims.quote: The spellings in the books are canon.
claims.page: list of principles, body of the post

claims.claim: Peterson reports that in Martin's Dothraki material the letters p and b occur only in the two names Pono and Bharbo.
claims.source: David J. Peterson, 'Developing Canon', Dothraki.com, 18 March 2012
claims.quote: In the names Pono and Bharbo

claims.claim: Peterson describes the Dothraki in Martin's books as a body of material that already existed before he began work on the language.
claims.source: David J. Peterson, 'Developing Canon', Dothraki.com, 18 March 2012
claims.quote: the Dothraki that existed in the books before I took

claims.claim: HBO's 2010 press release credits the Dothraki language with a vocabulary of more than 1,800 words at the time of the announcement.
claims.source: HBO official press release, dothraki.conlang.org, 12 April 2010
claims.quote: extensive vocabulary of more than 1,800 words

claims.claim: HBO's press release says Peterson drew on Martin's description of the language rather than on a vocabulary Martin had supplied.
claims.source: HBO official press release, dothraki.conlang.org, 12 April 2010
claims.quote: drew inspiration from George R.R. Martin’s description of the language

claims.claim: Wikipedia, relaying the HBO press release, states Peterson delivered over 1700 words to HBO before the initial shooting, a figure the press release itself puts at more than 1,800.
claims.source: Wikipedia 'Dothraki language' relaying the HBO press release of 12 April 2010
claims.quote: He delivered over 1700 words to HBO before the initial shooting.

claims.claim: Knippling argues Martin's main point-of-view character in each book holds an undistinguished share of chapters in the first half and dominates the second.
claims.source: DeAnna Knippling, Wonderland Press, 'A Song of Ice and Fire: Structure/Word Count Case Study'
claims.quote: comes to dominate the number of chapters in the latter half

claims.claim: Kirner-Ludwig concludes that the archaisms in the Game of Thrones scripted dialogues are not frequent in token terms yet are highly salient.
claims.quote: may not be particularly frequent token-wise, but are highly salient

claims.claim: Kirner-Ludwig states that Game of Thrones does not overdo pseudo-archaisms or archaic pronouns.
claims.quote: GoT does not overdo the use of pseudo-archaisms

claims.claim: Kirner-Ludwig's corpus is the full Game of Thrones transcripts covering 8 seasons and 73 episodes, analysed in Sketch Engine.
Kirner-Ludwig measures function words at about 43% of the Game of Thrones transcript corpus.
claims.quote: Function words make up for ca. 43% of the corpus

claims.claim: Kirner-Ludwig finds that only 7.6% of the transcripts' lexical word stock belongs to the medieval and fantasy-medieval semantic fields she investigated.
claims.quote: only 7.6% responded to the lexico-semantic fields

claims.claim: Kirner-Ludwig measures 42,426 tokens, 8.38% of her corpus, as names of persons, places and languages.
claims.quote: 42,426 tokens (8.38%) cover names of persons, places and languages
